journals.title: A fresh start
journals.prompt: An owner transfers £2,500 into a new business bank account as capital. Build the journal.
journals.hint: Bank is an asset increasing. Owner funding increases equity, not sales.
journals.explanation: Dr Bank £2,500; Cr Capital £2,500. Both assets and equity increase.

journals.title: Goods now, payment later
journals.prompt: Buy £780 of goods for resale on credit. Use a periodic inventory system. Ignore VAT.
journals.hint: The goods are for resale and the supplier is still owed money.
journals.explanation: Dr Purchases £780; Cr Trade payables £780. No bank movement occurs on this date.

journals.title: Settle a supplier
journals.prompt: Pay £420 from bank towards an already-recorded supplier invoice.
journals.hint: Reduce the liability. Do not record the purchase a second time.
journals.explanation: Dr Trade payables £420; Cr Bank £420. Settlement reduces an existing obligation.

journals.title: A customer pays
journals.prompt: Receive £360 into bank from a customer whose credit sale was already recorded.
journals.hint: Swap one asset (customer debt) for another (bank).
journals.explanation: Dr Bank £360; Cr Trade receivables £360. Do not credit Sales again.

journals.title: Loan principal comes back
journals.prompt: Another business repays a loan you made. Receive £1,050 into bank: £1,000 principal and £50 interest. Use three lines.
journals.hint: Only £50 is income. The £1,000 clears an existing asset.
journals.explanation: Dr Bank £1,050; Cr Loan receivable £1,000; Cr Interest income £50. Credits total £1,050.

journals.title: Business and owner
journals.prompt: The sole trader withdraws £180 from the business bank for personal shopping.
journals.hint: A personal withdrawal is not an operating expense.
journals.explanation: Dr Drawings £180; Cr Bank £180. Equity falls, but profit is unaffected.

journals.title: The unused policy
journals.prompt: Insurance expense includes £1,200 paid on 1 October for 12 months. At 31 December, adjust the unused part. Assume even monthly cover.
journals.hint: Nine of twelve months remain unused. Move that amount out of expense.

journals.title: The missing electricity cost
journals.prompt: At year-end, £275 of electricity has been used but not yet billed, paid or recorded. Enter the adjustment.
journals.hint: Recognise the expense and the obligation; do not touch bank.
journals.explanation: Dr Electricity expense £275; Cr Accruals £275. The cost belongs to this reporting period.

journals.title: A service still owed
journals.prompt: Sales includes a £600 receipt, of which £200 relates to services to be provided next year. Enter the year-end adjustment.
journals.hint: Remove the unearned portion from sales and show a liability.
journals.explanation: Dr Sales £200; Cr Income received in advance £200. The business still owes the service.

journals.title: Share the equipment cost
journals.prompt: Equipment costs £8,000, residual value £800 and useful life 4 years. Record a full year's straight-line depreciation.
journals.hint: Divide cost less residual value by useful life. There is no cash payment now.
journals.explanation: (£8,000 − £800) ÷ 4 = £1,800. Dr Depreciation expense; Cr Accumulated depreciation.

journals.title: Plan for warranty claims
journals.prompt: 2,000 products are sold with warranties. Expected claim rate is 2%; average claim costs £25. There is no existing provision. Record the expected obligation.
journals.hint: Products × expected claim rate × average cost per claim.
journals.explanation: 2,000 × 2% × £25 = £1,000. Dr Warranty expense; Cr Warranty provision.

journals.title: Split the repayment
journals.prompt: Pay £220 from bank on a loan. The payment includes £200 principal and £20 interest. Build a three-line journal.
journals.hint: Principal reduces the loan; interest is a separate expense. Credit bank for all cash paid.
journals.explanation: Dr Loan payable £200; Dr Interest expense £20; Cr Bank £220. Total debits equal total credits.

journals.title: Remove the original cost
journals.prompt: Equipment with original cost £4,000 and accumulated depreciation £2,600 is sold for £1,200. Enter ONLY the first disposal step: transfer original cost to Disposal.
journals.hint: The cost account is removed at original cost, not carrying amount or proceeds.
journals.explanation: Dr Disposal £4,000; Cr Equipment cost £4,000. Transferring depreciation, proceeds and the £200 loss are separate steps.

journals.title: Release a deferred grant
journals.prompt: A £9,000 grant was previously deferred and supports three equal years of qualifying costs. Conditions are met. Release one full year's income under the assumed deferral model.
journals.hint: Reduce the liability by the portion now earned; no new cash arrives.
journals.explanation: £9,000 ÷ 3 = £3,000. Dr Deferred grant income; Cr Grant income.

ledgers.title: Bank: a week in a new business
ledgers.intro: Use debit-positive signed arithmetic, then display Dr or Cr. Each row gives the journal movement already posted to Bank. Work out the balance after every row.
ledgers.hint: Start with £1,000 Dr. Add each debit and subtract each credit; a negative result is a Cr balance.
ledgers.explanation: Closing Bank is £750 Dr. Receipts increase the asset by debits; payments reduce it by credits.

ledgers.title: Trade payables: follow the supplier
ledgers.intro: A payable normally has a credit balance. The opening balance is £800 Cr. Use the actual posted Dr and Cr columns to update it.
ledgers.hint: Treat the opening credit as −£800 in your calculation. Debits move it towards zero; credits make more owed.
ledgers.explanation: Balances are £1,300 Cr, £600 Cr, £850 Cr, then nil. The final payment clears the payable.

ledgers.title: Bank: crossing into an overdraft
ledgers.intro: A bank balance can cross from debit to credit. A credit bank balance represents an overdraft; it does not become an expense.
ledgers.hint: Do not stop at zero: £300 − £500 is −£200, displayed £200 Cr.
ledgers.explanation: Balances: £200 Cr, £100 Cr, £250 Cr, £350 Dr. Each receipt reduces an overdraft before creating a debit balance.

ledgers.title: Disposal: clear an asset sale
ledgers.intro: Follow a disposal account for an asset costing £6,000 with £4,000 accumulated depreciation, sold for £1,500. Use Dr for nil balances in this activity.
ledgers.hint: Original cost is a debit. Accumulated depreciation and proceeds are credits. The final credit transfers the loss out.
ledgers.explanation: The balances are £6,000 Dr, £2,000 Dr, £500 Dr, then nil. The £500 debit before closing represented a loss.

trialBalances.title: A trader's first balances
trialBalances.intro: Enter the magnitude and Dr/Cr side of every ledger closing balance. Amounts are given without sides; infer each normal side from the account type. All balances are normal in this set.
trialBalances.hint: Assets, expenses and drawings normally go in Dr; equity, liabilities and sales normally go in Cr.
trialBalances.explanation: Debits £10,400 = credits £10,400. Agreement checks arithmetic but not complete omissions or wrong-account errors.

trialBalances.title: After the year-end adjustments
trialBalances.intro: Place each closing balance on its normal side and enter its amount. This set includes prepayments, accruals and a contra-asset.
trialBalances.hint: Accumulated depreciation is a credit, prepayments a debit and accruals a credit.
trialBalances.explanation: Both columns total £15,800. The equipment's cost and accumulated depreciation appear separately in the trial balance.

trialBalances.title: Do not assume Bank is always a debit
trialBalances.intro: Enter each amount and side. Bank is explicitly a £250 OVERDRAFT (Cr); all other balances are normal. The actual ledger balance overrides the usual side.
trialBalances.hint: The overdraft is a credit. Drawings remain a debit, not an operating expense.
trialBalances.explanation: Debits and credits each total £4,850. An overdraft appears in the credit column despite bank normally being an asset account.

exams.title: A small trader: records to gross profit
exams.scenario: Original first-year practice, not an official Glasgow paper. A new sole trader introduces £5,000 into bank, buys equipment £1,000 from bank, purchases 100 goods at £8 each on credit, sells 60 for £15 each on credit and receives £600 from those customers. There is no opening inventory, VAT or other transaction. Use periodic inventory accounting; all unsold goods are undamaged.

parts.prompt: Prepare journals for all five transactions. Include account names, sides and amounts.
parts.solution: Capital: Dr Bank £5,000; Cr Capital £5,000. Equipment: Dr Equipment £1,000; Cr Bank £1,000. Goods: Dr Purchases £800; Cr Trade payables £800. Sale: Dr Trade receivables £900; Cr Sales £900. Receipt: Dr Bank £600; Cr Trade receivables £600. Award up to 2 marks per correct balanced entry.

parts.prompt: Calculate closing Bank and Trade receivables, giving Dr/Cr sides.
parts.solution: Bank £5,000 − £1,000 + £600 = £4,600 Dr (2 marks). Trade receivables £900 − £600 = £300 Dr (2 marks). Customer collection is not new sales.

parts.prompt: Calculate closing inventory, cost of sales and gross profit. Explain why all purchases are not cost of sales.
parts.solution: Closing inventory 40 × £8 = £320 (2). Cost of sales 60 × £8 = £480 (1). Revenue 60 × £15 = £900; gross profit £900 − £480 = £420 (2). Unsold goods remain an asset rather than an expense of this period (1).

exams.title: Year-end: whose expense is it?
exams.scenario: Original practice based on the supplied adjustment topics. Year-end is 31 December. Insurance £2,400 was paid on 1 September for 12 months and fully charged to expense. Electricity of £350 for December is unrecorded and unpaid. Sales includes £900 received for services: £600 is earned this year and £300 relates to next year. Ignore VAT and tax.

parts.prompt: Show an insurance timeline calculation and prepare the prepayment adjustment.
parts.solution: Monthly cost £200 (1). Four months September–December used, expense £800 (2). Eight unused months give £1,600 prepayment (1). Dr Prepayments £1,600; Cr Insurance expense £1,600 (2).

parts.prompt: Prepare the electricity accrual and income-in-advance journals.
parts.solution: Dr Electricity expense £350; Cr Accruals £350 (3). Dr Sales £300; Cr Income received in advance £300 (3). Neither adjustment changes bank.

parts.prompt: Calculate the combined change in profit from the unadjusted figures. State the assets and liabilities created.
parts.solution: Insurance expense falls £1,600, electricity expense rises £350, sales falls £300. Net profit increases £950 (4 including workings). A current prepayment asset £1,600 arises (2); current liabilities are accruals £350 and income in advance £300 (2).

exams.title: A van disposal & asset note
exams.scenario: Original first-year practice, not a past paper. Motor vehicles have opening cost £30,000 and accumulated depreciation £12,000. Additions in the year cost £8,000. One van costing £10,000 is sold for £3,500; accumulated depreciation on that van at disposal is £6,000. The total depreciation charge for the year is £4,000 and already includes any depreciation to the sale date. Do not calculate extra depreciation.

parts.prompt: Find the van's carrying amount at disposal and the gain or loss.
parts.solution: Carrying amount £10,000 − £6,000 = £4,000 (2). Proceeds £3,500 are £500 below carrying amount: loss £500 (2).

parts.prompt: Show all four disposal journals, including the closing transfer.
parts.solution: Dr Disposal £10,000; Cr Vehicles cost £10,000. Dr Accumulated depreciation £6,000; Cr Disposal £6,000. Dr Bank £3,500; Cr Disposal £3,500. Dr Loss on disposal £500; Cr Disposal £500. 2 marks per correct entry.

parts.prompt: Prepare cost and accumulated depreciation movements; give closing and opening NBV.

exams.title: Inventory, warranties & finance
exams.scenario: Original mixed-topic practice. Inventory: buy 20 units at £5 and 10 at £8, then sell 24 units at £12. NRV exceeds cost. Warranty sales (a separate product line): 2,000 units, expected claim rate 3%, average claim cost £20; no opening provision. Loan: £2,400 borrowed and repaid in 12 instalments of £220. For this question ONLY, allocate total interest equally across the instalments. Ignore VAT and fees.

parts.prompt: For the inventory line, calculate cost of sales, closing inventory and gross profit using FIFO and periodic AVCO.
parts.solution: Revenue 24 × £12 = £288. FIFO cost of sales (20 × £5) + (4 × £8) = £132; closing inventory 6 × £8 = £48; gross profit £156 (5 marks for FIFO with workings). Periodic AVCO £180 ÷ 30 = £6 per unit; cost of sales £144; inventory £36; gross profit £144 (5 for AVCO with workings).

parts.prompt: Calculate and journal the warranty provision. Then journal £100 of covered claims paid.
parts.solution: Expected cost 2,000 × 3% × £20 = £1,200 (2). Dr Warranty expense £1,200; Cr Warranty provision £1,200 (2). Dr Warranty provision £100; Cr Bank £100 (2).

parts.prompt: Find total interest, monthly interest and principal under the stated assumption, then journal one repayment. Explain why the assumption matters.
parts.solution: Total repayments £2,640; total interest £240 (2). Monthly interest £20; principal £200 (2). Dr Loan payable £200; Dr Interest expense £20; Cr Bank £220 (2). Equal allocation is a simplified assumption; an effective-interest approach instead applies the periodic effective rate to the opening balance (2).
